title.en: Exploring forces: push, pull, friction and gravity

text.en: Sonali and Ragini cycle on a windy day. The wind pushes against them, and going uphill feels harder than on flat ground. What is acting on the bicycles?

A push or a pull on an object is called a force.
A force can change the speed of an object, its direction of motion, or its shape.
Stopping a moving bicycle with brakes changes speed, hitting a ball with a bat changes direction, and pressing a balloon changes shape.
Contact forces act when objects touch, like muscular force and friction.
Non-contact forces act from a distance, like gravity, magnetic force and electrostatic force.
Friction acts between surfaces in contact and opposes motion, which is why a wet surface is slippery and brakes work on rough surfaces.
Friction can be increased by roughness, as in tyre treads, and reduced by smoothness or lubricants like oil.
Gravity pulls every object towards the Earth, which is why a ball thrown up comes down.
A magnet attracts iron from a distance and a rubbed comb picks up paper bits, which are magnetic and electrostatic forces.
If an object is at rest, forces on it may be balancing one another, which we study more in higher grades.

problem.en: Name the force and its effect: a footballer kicks a ball.

text.en: The kick is a push, a contact force.
The ball speeds up and changes direction.
Gravity and friction then bring it down and slow it.

prompt.en: Why is it easier to slip on a wet floor?

commonMisconceptions.en: Gravity is less on wet floors.

points.en: Force is a push or pull that changes speed, direction or shape.
Contact forces: muscular, friction. Non-contact: gravity, magnetic, electrostatic.
Friction opposes motion; roughness raises it, lubricants lower it.
